query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high-entropy alloy protective coatings is governed by the in situ formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, adaptive surface layer (often accompanied by favorable reactive oxide phases) during sliding, which enhances hardness and reduces friction.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or similar) with a relatively coarse-grained, single-phase microstructure before wear exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled variation in the initial grain size or alloy composition (by, for instance, adjusting processing parameters to yield a finer or coarser microstructure) intended to modify the ease of dynamic grain refinement and reactive oxide formation during sliding.
generation.conditions: Wear tests performed under controlled sliding conditions (e.g., constant load and speed) in an inert or low-oxidation environment to minimize environmental effects; this should be compared to a baseline coating with larger-grained microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer (possibly containing reactive oxide nanocomposites) that serves as a barrier to further material removal through enhanced hardness and favorable frictional behavior.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, local high shear and frictional heating trigger dynamic amorphization and grain refinement, possibly coupled with limited reactive oxidation. This leads to the development of a dense, ultra-fine (adaptive) surface layer which increases resistance to deformation and wear while reducing friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings engineered to favor the formation of this ultra-nanocrystalline layer will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline coarse-grained coatings. In microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM or STEM), a distinct gradient with an ultra-fine surface layer should be observable post-test.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy coating with a standard (coarse-grained) microstructure that does not readily develop an adaptive, refined near-surface layer under identical wear testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA protective coatings in wear applications under conditions where the shear and thermal inputs are sufficient to trigger dynamic microstructural transformations, typically in inert or low-oxidizing environments. Extreme sliding or oxidizing conditions may introduce competing mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the extent of grain refinement (or oxide nanocomposite formation) and the degree of friction and wear reduction is not precisely defined, and its dependence on alloy composition beyond model systems remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings—one with processing parameters designed to promote ultra-fine initial microstructure (thus facilitating the dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer under wear) and one with a coarse-grained baseline structure. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in an inert atmosphere. Use systematic TEM/STEM analysis to measure near-surface grain size evolution and perform friction and wear rate measurements.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear testing
Post-test surface microstructure characterizations (grain size distribution via TEM/STEM, evidence for oxide phases via XRD/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings that are designed to favor the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline adaptive surface layer do not show significantly lower friction and wear rates than the coarse-grained baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected refined layer (or its formation is not correlated with improved performance), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces

Abstract: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. The reactive wear protection strategy offers a pathway for designing ultra-wear resistant alloys
